messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Construction Worker
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Hopelessness: I have no future, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Nadia is a 36-year-old married Middle Eastern American woman who works on a construction crew, a job she had always valued for its physical rhythm, clear tasks, and the pride she took in keeping pace with the men around her. The event she returns to when describing the start of her difficulties was not an accident at work but a sudden, life-threatening illness that unfolded with the same brutal force she usually associated with job-site emergencies. She became acutely ill over a short period, and what she remembers most is how quickly her body stopped feeling like something she knew. She recalls the panic of being unable to trust what was happening inside her, the sense that her condition was worsening while people moved urgently around her, and the fear that she might die before anyone could stop it. In her memory, the experience is bound up with bright lights, rushed voices, the hard surfaces of the hospital, and the terrifying realization that no amount of strength, endurance, or willpower could make her body obey her.

Afterward, Nadia expected to feel grateful simply to have survived, and at first she tried to act as though she had put it behind her. Instead, she found herself living as if some further medical disaster were just about to strike. At night she lay awake for long stretches, unable to settle, her body taut and restless in bed beside her husband. If she did fall asleep, she woke easily, already tense, as though she had been bracing through the night. During the day she noticed how quickly she startled. A sudden bang from dropped lumber, the metallic crack of tools, or a coworker stepping up behind her on site could make her whole body jolt before she had time to think. She hated how visible this felt, especially in a work environment where she was used to presenting herself as steady and tough. Even when nothing obvious was wrong, she moved through the day with the sense that her muscles were clenched for danger, her body waiting for something bad to happen again.

Because the illness had come from inside her own body, what frightened Nadia most was not only the memory of nearly dying but the feeling that she could no longer trust herself. She had come to believe that bad things could happen to her without warning and that she had no real way to stop them. When she felt keyed up, unable to sleep, or suddenly shaken by a noise, she did not see these as understandable reactions to what she had lived through. Instead, she was certain that something was seriously wrong with her mind. There were moments when she thought, I am going crazy. At other times the future felt blank to her. She spoke as though the illness had cut her life into a before and after, and after it there was only uncertainty. It was hard for her to picture growing older, making plans, or trusting that ordinary life would continue.

Over the months that followed, Nadia coped by keeping herself occupied as relentlessly as she could. She took extra shifts, volunteered for physically exhausting tasks, and stayed busy even once she got home, telling herself that if she kept moving there would be less space for her mind to go where it wanted to go. On the construction site this meant throwing herself into work with a kind of grim intensity, focusing on measurements, materials, cleanup, anything concrete. Her coworkers saw that she was hardworking, but her husband noticed that she had become harder to reach. At home she often ate more than usual, especially in the evenings, using food to blunt the edge of her feelings and fill the hours when sleep would not come. She also described going emotionally flat, shutting down rather than letting herself feel frightened or overwhelmed. This numbing created distance in her marriage; her husband would ask what was wrong, and she would tell him she was fine or too tired to talk, even when she was lying awake beside him, rigid and alert.

By the time she sought help, Nadia was exhausted by the effort it took to get through each day. What finally pushed her to come in was the combination of chronic sleeplessness, the sense that her body never stood down, and her growing fear that these reactions meant she was losing her mind. She was also troubled by how narrow her life had become: work, distraction, eating, and trying not to feel. Sitting in the office, she spoke plainly but with visible strain, as if even naming the experience risked setting something off in her. She said she wanted to know whether it was possible to live without feeling constantly braced and whether she could ever believe again that her life was not already over.
